newsitem.title: UK: Investors lap up State Bank of India issue.
newsitem.headline: Investors lap up State Bank of India issue.

text.p: Despite a poor year for Indian shares, foreign investors ploughed money into a global share offering for the country's largest bank, State Bank of India.

The global depositary receipt (GDR) issue was priced at $14.15 per GDR, a premium of 4.8 percent over the underlying share, despite a bear market which has seen the ING Barings Indian GDR index fall nearly 17 percent this year.
The GDRs represent two underlying SBI shares. The underlying closed share closed at 251.25 rupees in Bombay on Thursday, deal managers Lehman Brothers and Merrill Lynch said in a statement.

The average market premium investors are prepared to pay for dollar-denominated Indian GDRs, which avoid direct rupee exposure and the settlement hassles of the local market, has slipped from over 20 percent at the start of the year to less than nine percent now.
SBI had always been regarded as an issue that could beat the Indian bear market, which has seen a number of high profile cancellations such as Saw Pipes and Gujarat Alkalies.

Investors and syndicates had expected 1996 to be a bonanza year after a poor 1995 which saw just four issues worth $235 million from India, following 1994's 40 issues worth $3.0 billion, but dreams crumbled as the Indian market fell sharply after a bright start to the year. The Bombay Sensex 30-share index is down over seven percent since the start of 1996.
There was around $900 million in applications for the issue, which comprised 24.735 million GDRs.
"It was a phenomenal result," said a spokesman for Lehman Brothers.
